utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. The affirmation still applies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Yes, I understand that it does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bezruchenko, I'd like to move to a different topic right now. During cross-examination you were shown a number of media reports and other documents which describe the actions of the NLA in the first part of 2001 as "terrorist attacks," and which described the NLA as terrorists. For example, you were shown what is now Exhibit 1D254, which is a statement from the foreign affairs committee of the European parliament on the 20th of March, 2001. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, do we have a technical problem or should I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We are being entertained with another case on the screen. But apart from that, we have no technical problem. Continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bezruchenko, during the course of researching and writing your expert report, did you also review documents that addressed the international community's reaction to the situation in Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we please show the witness what is Exhibit 1D256. Your Honours, this is a report prepared by the International Crisis Group dated the 5th of April, 2001. And it's titled The Macedonian Question, Reform or Rebellion, and my colleague addressed this page at pages 7046 to 7047 of the transcript. Perhaps if we could simply turn to the back of this report, what is Annex C to it and which has ERN number N002-5194.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Bezruchenko, this is an appendix to that report and it's a description of what the International Crisis Group is and what it does. And you see it says at the top it's a private multi-national organisation committed to strengthening the capacity of the international community to anticipate, understand, and act to prevent and contain conflict. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Below that, the next paragraph we see the ICG's approach is grounded in field research done by teams of political analysts. In the next paragraph we see that the ICG's reports are distributed widely to officials in foreign ministries and international organisations and then at the end of that third paragraph we see the following: "The ICG is chaired by former Finnish president Martti Ahtisaari and former Australian foreign minister Gareth Evans has been president and chief executive since January of 2000." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we can turn now, please, to what is page 6 of the report itself and it has ERN number N002-5178. It has -- it also has ERN 1D00-6441. And if we could focus on the bottom half of this page, please. Mr. Bezruchenko, we see a subtitle 3, Tetovo, eruption of violence. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And the last sentence of the next paragraph says the following: "On 13 March a rebel group claiming to be members of the National Liberation Army, NLA, began firing at Macedonian police officers in Tetovo from high positions in the Sar mountains around the city." Are you following me?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we turn, please, to the next page. If we go to the top of the next page, please. And the top paragraph says this at the beginning: "Most political leaders were fully aware of the growing threat. In Autumn 2000, as the legitimate Albanian political parties continued, a small group of rebels or guerillas again recruiting in north-western Macedonia." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So, so far, can you agree with me that the International Crisis Group is referring to the early members of the NLA, not as terrorists but as rebels or guerillas?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we can scroll down, please, two paragraphs. You see there's a paragraph there, Mr. Bezruchenko, beginning with: "On 21 March." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And that paragraph begins: "On 21 March, the government gave the rebels a 24-hour deadline to lay down their arms." The next sentence: "The rebels initially responded with a unilateral cease-fire." The next sentence: "The government rejected any negotiations with 'terrorists' and the Macedonian military offensive began on the early morning of 25 March." And then, according to the ICG, the following day the government announced that the rebels had been flushed out of a string of villages above the city. Are you following me?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: In the next paragraph, the bottom paragraph, in the second sentence you see a reference to the rebel guerillas. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So, so far in this report, the only reference to terrorists is a reference made apparently by the Macedonia government. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we turn to the next page, please. It's page 8 of the report. If we can scroll up to the top. And that top paragraph says: "The Macedonian troops met little resistance and proceeded to pour shells on mostly civilian houses where the guerillas were thought to have been holed up." And then later on in that paragraph: "Be this as it may, most of the guerillas dispersed in the first hours of the offensive." Can we scroll down to the third paragraph of that page, please. Mr. Bezruchenko, the first paragraph says: "International observers on both sides" -- excuse me. This is first sentence of the third paragraph. Says: "International observers on both sides of the Macedonia/Kosovo border are less confident that the insurgents have been defeated. Are you following me?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if you look at the last sentence of that paragraph the International Crisis Group says: "It is hard to believe these guerilla fighters will now slink off to Kosovo, not to be heard of again." So, so far, again, no reference to the word "terrorists" coming from the International Crisis Group. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we turn to what is page 14 of this report. It bears ERN number 1D00-6449. It's page 14 of the report. And, Mr. Bezruchenko, you see at the bottom of the page there's a Roman numeral V followed by the subtitle, conclusions. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And the first paragraph of the conclusions was read to you by my colleague, refers to the loosely coordinated guerilla cells. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The next paragraph, we see a reference to rebel fighters. And apart from the reference made by the government of the Macedonia referred to in quotes as "terrorists," did you see any reference or any label of the NLA as terrorists or committing terrorist actions in this report?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. It is the suggestion of Mr. Saxon that there is none, or simply that the evidence is that Mr. Bezruchenko hasn't seen any. We would like to be clear about what's the position of the Prosecution in relation to this report. We understand that there are in fact discussion at the beginning of the report, but if the only question that was raised with Mr. Bezruchenko is if indeed he had seen any reference in the passage read to him, it's clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I would suggest, Mr. Mettraux, that is clearly playing with words. I think the meaning can be detected below the words. And carry on Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you. And, Your Honour, apparently I am also being entertained now by the transcript of another case. It is probably more interesting than my re-direct examination, but if I could have that corrected, I would be grateful.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bezruchenko, during cross-examination my colleague showed you what is now Exhibit 1D262, which was a media article from Radio Free Europe from the 15th of March, 2001. And this was at pages 7055 to 7057 of the transcript. And it's an article about some comments made by United States Ambassador James Pardew about the situation at that time in Macedonia. And in that, Mr. Pardew is mentioned in this article as condemning the violence that was occurring in Macedonia and referring to the NLA as a small group of extremists who are simply trying to use intimidation and violence to promote their own political agenda. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And my colleague asked you whether this statement was the expression of the view of the ambassador of one of the most powerful states in the world, about what their understanding of the situation in Macedonia was at that time. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'd like to show you, Mr. Bezruchenko, what Mr. Pardew, Ambassador Pardew, and some other representatives and figures of the United States said about the situation in Macedonia a few months later on the 13th of June, 2001 at a hearing before the Committee on Foreign Relations in the United States Senate and if we could please show the witness what is now Exhibit 1D228, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, this particular exhibit has very small font, very small print, and so the Prosecution has brought some extra copies to assist the Judges and the other parties in following along and to hope reduce some strain on your eyes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: As can you see, this is a hearing before the United States Senate on the 13th of June, 2001 and the title of the proceedings, the name of the proceedings is, the crisis in Macedonia and US engagement in the Balkans. And if we can turn, please, to what is a statement made by Ambassador James Pardew which begins at page 1D00-6284, which is page 7 of this committee report. And if we could focus on the bottom half of this page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bezruchenko, on the bottom half of this page we see Ambassador Pardew making a statement to this Senate Committee. And in the second and third paragraphs of this statement he says the following: "Macedonia remains critical for regional security and stability. The current conflict there must be resolved. However, no purely military approach can succeed here. Efforts to quell the armed insurgency must take place, therefore, within the framework of political measures that advance Macedonia along the path of necessary democratic, social, and economic reforms." Mr. Bezruchenko, in the next paragraph James Pardew says this: "The situation today" - this is 13 June - "in Macedonian is precarious. The insurgent National Liberation Army, NLA, launched its first attacks in north-west Macedonia in February. Since then, the fighting has continued off and on largely in ethnic Albanian areas." Can you agree, Mr. Bezruchenko, so far you don't see Ambassador Pardew referring to the NLA as terrorists, do you?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see Ambassador Pardew as referring to the NLA as terrorists, I don't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You don't -- do you see him here referring to the NLA as committing terrorist attacks?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we can turn to the next page, please. And in the first full paragraph, now what is page 8 of the committee hearing, Ambassador Pardew says that: "The government of Macedonia has a responsibility to protect its territory and citizens, but it must respond to extremist provocation in a measured and proportionate way that protects the lives of civilians." Are you following me?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Two paragraphs down begins with: "The ongoing military stand-off makes all the more urgent the need for progress on the political front." And then the next sentence says this: "We welcome President Trajkovski's plan for defusing the insurgency approved by their parliament yesterday." So, so far, we see Ambassador Pardew going so far as to refer, apparently, to NLA as extremists. Is that right.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: But also refers to them as an insurgency.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: He does not refer to them as terrorists?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. He doesn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we can scroll to the bottom of this page, please. You see the paragraph beginning with: "On the security track." Do you see that, Mr. Bezruchenko?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The last sentence of that paragraph says this: "The United Nations in Kosovo has recently promulgated tough new regulations on weapons possession and illegal border crossing that enhance the UN and NATO's ability to deal with the insurgency and its supporters." Does it appear to you that now at least on the 13th of June Ambassador Pardew is recognizing that there is an insurgency taking place in Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bezruchenko, do you know whether Ambassador Pardew, James Pardew, subsequently played a role in brokering the Ohrid Framework Agreement?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I think his involvement was very significant.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we can turn, please, to the page that bears the ERN in the bottom right-hand corner, 1D00-6291. And it's page 14 of this committee report. And if we can focus, please, on the bottom half of this page, and Your Honours you will see a reference here to the chairman speaking. The chairman in this case, the chairman of this committee at that time was Senator Joseph Biden.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bezruchenko I'd like you to focus on the very last paragraph on this page. And Ambassador Pardew is answering a question from the chairman, Senator Biden, and that paragraph starts: "Beginning in February." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: This is one paragraph before a paragraph that my colleague Mr. Mettraux read to you at page 7108 of the transcript last Wednesday. And this paragraph says: "Beginning in February, while most of everyone's attention was focussed on southern Serbia and the insurgency that was going on there, a group of extremists - exactly whether they were from Macedonia or originated in Kosovo is not quite clear - began to form and to take military action against the government forces in north-west Macedonia." Are you following me, Mr. Bezruchenko?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So here, Ambassador Pardew is referring to military action rather than terrorist action. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And then we see the paragraph that my colleague read to you last week. It begins with a short sentence: "That insurgency group." And so again, we see the ambassador referring to the NLA, apparently, as an insurgency. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's fair.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Two sentences down there is a -- excuse me. Two paragraphs down there is a -- there's a paragraph beginning with the phrase: "Its strategy is the same strategy." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And the last sentence of that paragraph says: "So we are very concerned about these military operations." You see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Now, Ambassador Pardew uses the term "military operations," not "terrorist operations." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, we'd simply object to that. I believe that the second sentence should be read in the context of the first sentence which refers to the military response by the Macedonian authorities. I believe that the expression "military operations" refer to the response, not the original attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, different people can read this different ways. But the first sentence appears to the Prosecution to express concern that the strategy of the NLA is to provoke a repressive military response and to gain support from that response from the population. So a fair reading of that last sentence is that the Ambassador Pardew is concerned about these military operations, perhaps on both parts, the NLA and the government of Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: In due course, should it be still thought material, the Chamber may have to consider these disparate views. For the moment it is enough that each view is open. So we will hear if the witness is able to throw any light on it, rather than counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bezruchenko, in that paragraph, as a military analyst, are you able to comment on the scope of the concerns of Ambassador Pardew?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apparently this concern was quite significant and justified on the grounds of spreading out violence in northern Macedonia, as well as the military operations which were taking place there at that time by -- which were conducted by both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we can turn, please, to what is ERN 1D00-6306, please. It's page 29 of the committee's report. Mr. Bezruchenko, do you remember a man named General Wesley Clark?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you recall during the late 1990s what position General Clark held?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: He held a number of positions, in fact. He was the supreme commander, NATO Europe and he also was running the operations in Bosnia and Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And do you know what army he at that time was a member of?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a member of the US army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, I'm sorry, I can't read the -- perhaps I can. You say he was running the operations in Bosnia and Kosovo, General Clark. If we could be a little bit more specific. What involvement did General Clark have, if any, in the armed conflict in Kosovo and the rest of Serbia in 1999?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as we know, KFOR actually entered Kosovo in 1999 and I think General Clark was involved in running the operations related to KFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And how about during the armed conflict itself in 1999?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: He -- before that, he was the senior military official of NATO who was in charge of NATO operations in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: We see here on this page that General Wesley Clark also gave a statement to the Committee on Foreign Relations of the US Senate on the 13th of June, 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if we can turn, please, to the next page. And if we could focus on the last part of this page, please, the bottom part.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: We see here that General Clark provided a prepared statement to the committee of United States Senators, and in the last paragraph, Mr. Bezruchenko, General Clark says the following: "In fact, we are once against at a critical juncture in the further evolution of events there," that is in the Balkans, "as we witness the tragic escalation of fighting in Macedonia and once again, as the international community attempts to resolve an emerging conflict, with limited diplomatic missions and exhortations to restraint, the lessons of recent history run square against the pressures of contemporary politics. And the last sentence says -- excuse me. The last two sentences say: "But all the pleas and counsel of the European Union and NATO political leaders have not and cannot end the fighting there. And as the fighting continues, the familiar pattern of excessive use of force and needless harm to innocent civilians has reappeared, promising that the continuation of conflict will make any political solution increasingly difficult between increasingly alienated hostile and ethnic groups." Now do you see there any reference to the NLA as a terrorist group?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we turn to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir, which page is it going to be now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It will be 1D00-6308. It says page 31 at the top of the text. It was the following page from where you just where.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if we can review the bottom part of this page, please, the very last paragraph, if we can focus on that. Here General Clark tells the US Senate committee: "At this point it seems clear that the situation on the ground is going to continue to deteriorate unless NATO actively intervenes. The troops of the Macedonian army lack the equipment, skills and leadership to meet the challenge posed by the Albanian fighters. Their continuing efforts to resist rebel incursions appear to have done little more than destroy civilian property and convince thousands to flee their homes and villages." Are you following me, Mr. Bezruchenko?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Now, General Clark has used the term Albanian fighters and he's used the term rebel, and rebel incursions. Have you seen that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Has he used here any reference to terrorist?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bezruchenko, General Clark is urging intervention by NATO in the situation in Macedonia, saying that the conflict or the situation would not be resolved without the use of NATO forces. What does that tell us about the level and complexity of the fighting in Macedonia as of June 2001?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: My assessment is that as of June 2001 the situation was indeed extremely precarious. The NLA was an advance and the Macedonian government did not have sufficient resources, in terms of weapons and equipment to counter this situation. Apparently the NATO involvement was in the order of the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we can turn, please, to the next page. Actually, I will move on. I will move on at this point. If we can turn to what is page -- has ERN 1D00-6310. It says 33 at the top of the text. And if we could focus on the bottom of the page, please. Your Honours, this is the beginning of a statement by a man named Richard Perle to the United States Senate committee. Richard Perle was a former assistant secretary of Defence of the United States and at the time I believe he was a member of a research institute in Washington called the American Enterprise Institute.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bezruchenko, if you could focus your mind, please, on the last paragraph on this page, the second sentence says: "Macedonia today looks very much like Croatia, Bosnia and Kosovo." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What happened in those regions during the 1990s?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: These regions were in fact devastated by horrible civil wars which were raging there following the disintegration and dissolution of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we turn to the next page, please. Mr. Pearl continues his remarks. If we could scroll up a bit to the -- thank you very much. Mr. Bezruchenko, the third paragraph on this page begins with the word "last." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And in this paragraph Mr. Pearl says the following: "Last let me say that a delay, even by days or weeks, in coming to grips with the current situation in Macedonia could prove disastrous. It is not often that things move so rapidly that one feels compelled to say immediate action is necessary. But as I understand the situation in Macedonia today, there is a very great danger that the combination of guerilla attacks and an unsophisticated response," and then it goes on to say "will create the kind of polarisation and radicalisation that would turn Macedonia into a catastrophe, like Croatia, Bosnia and Kosovo." Mr. Bezruchenko, we see here a reference to guerrilla attacks. Is there any reference to terrorist attacks?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not see any.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we could focus on the next paragraph, please. The second sentence of the next paragraph reads like this: "As the Macedonian army struggles to deal with the insurgency, it is not a particularly well-trained army, not particularly effective in dealing with this type of insurgency." Does it appear that Richard Perle is referring or labelling the activities of the NLA as an insurgency?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we could show the witness, please, what is Rule 65 ter, Prosecution Rule 65 ter 953. Your Honours, this is a document -- it's another report by the International Crisis Group, dated 20th of June, 2001, it's entitled, Macedonia: The last chance for peace. And it was used by my learned colleague during cross-examination at pages 7116 to page 7117 of the transcript, and if we could turn, please, to what is the -- the executive summary of this report, it has ERN number N002-5227. And if we could make that text perhaps a little bit bigger. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bezruchenko, the first sentence of the first paragraph of the Executive Summary says: "In the past three months, since mid-March 2001, Macedonia has stared in the abyss of interethnic conflict, pulled away from the precipice, squandered opportunities for a political settlement, then returned as if sleepwalking to the brink of civil war." Are you following me?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The last sentence of that paragraph refers to -- it says: "For their part the NLA guerrillas expressed a readiness to halt their insurgency but want to see concrete steps towards improving Albanian rights." Here again the International Crisis Group seems to be referring to the NLA activities as an insurgency and the members of the NLA as guerrillas. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is what it seems to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if we could now show the witness what is page 3 of the report itself, which bears ERN N002-5232. Mr. Bezruchenko, if we could focus on the first paragraph for a moment, please. You see in the middle of that paragraph there is -- that paragraph discusses how violence erupted in mid-February 2001. And then around -- and that was around Tanusevci. And then we see two sentences later: "Ethnic Albanian rebels in the zone needed to transfer into Macedonia." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If you could go two paragraphs down, please, to the paragraph that starts with the phrase: "The government reacted loudly." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That sentence says: "The government reacted loudly but irresolutely until 21 March 2001, when the rebels were given an ultimatum to disarm and/or leave the country or face a full-scale military offensive." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Again, does the International Crisis Group appear to be labelling the NLA as rebels and not terrorists?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm not sure if no is a comprehensible response to my question.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see that the --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... The International Crisis Group -- my question was, does the International Crisis Group appear to be labelling the NLA as rebels and not terrorists?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that the International Crisis Group appears to be labelling the NLA as terrorists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps for the sake of clarity of the record and perhaps also to expedite matter, Mr. Saxon could perhaps refer to footnote 2 of the report which explains the use of terminology by the ICG and by a number of other entities or political bodies, in any case. What the ICG makes it clear that the uses the terms insurgence, rebels guerillas and extremists interchangeably to describe the members of the NLA and it also points out that the US state department uses very specific criteria for applying the designation terrorist and that the US government defines the NLA as extremists using terrorist methods. This is at page 1 of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm grateful, Your Honour. I think that might be a matter for closing argument or it might have been a matter for cross-examination, but may I move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we turn to what is page 5 of this report, please. It has ERN number N002-5234.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: This is a section of this report, section 2, it's called the National Liberation Army. Mr. Bezruchenko, do you see in the second paragraph, the second paragraph begins this way: "The insurgents stole the political agenda of the country's elected Albanian leaders." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if we could also look, please, at the next page, page of the report. Mr. Bezruchenko, the third paragraph of page 6 says the following: "Albanians in Macedonia overwhelmingly support the stated objectives of the Albanian guerillas but disagree with their violent methods." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes I do, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And two sentences later we see: "The insurrection is, however, gaining support in villages, not in harm's way." From a military perspective what is an insurrection?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Insurrection could be described as a rebellion aimed to gain certain political goals and confined to one particular country or region.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Can we turn, please, to page 20 of this report. It has ERN number N002-5249. And if we could focus on the subtitle, conclusions and the paragraph below that, please. Mr. Bezruchenko, the first paragraph of the conclusions section says: "The country faces an insurgency that is largely domestic, which means that the fighters know the terrain, are committed to their cause and, without a political solution, are likely to fight on, despite losses. The Macedonian military and much of the public believe a victory was won in Tetovo at the end of March 2001. Yet the guerrillas were undefeated." Does this conclusion suggest that the NLA, at least as of the time of writing of this report, was going to continue fighting?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would seek to tender this report, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As exhibit P494, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bezruchenko, turning to another topic at page 7019 of the transcript, my colleague asked you some questions about the withdrawal of NLA units from the village of Aracinovo. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And also, on pages 7097 to 7102, you were also asked about the events in Aracinovo and casualties incurred there by the security forces of Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we show the witness, please, what is Prosecution 65 ter number 849.5. And if we could focus on the last half of this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: This is a media report dated the 23rd of June, 2001, from - my French is very poor - from the French press agency. And it's reported from near Aracinovo, Macedonia. And the first sentence says: "The Macedonian army stepped up its assault Saturday on ethnic Albanian rebels dug into a town on the edge of the capital Skopje, spurning a warning from NATO chief George Robertson that ditching a fragile truce was 'madness.'"? Are you following me, Mr. Bezruchenko?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Two paragraphs down we see that: Helicopter gun ships, tanks, heavy artillery and machine-guns fired into the centre of Aracinovo for a second day in the most concentrated attack on the rebels since the army drove them from the edge of Tetovo in the north-west in March." And on the last paragraph on this page we see that rockets from Ukrainian-made MR24 helicopters slammed into Aracinovo that had been held by the NLA since June the 8th. Could we move to the next page, please. The top of the next page, we see that tanks were seen moving in the area, and heavy artillery fired salvo after salvo at the NLA guerrillas dug in inside the town. And in the next paragraph we see that frequent automatic weapons and mortar fire signalled that the guerrillas were fighting back, despite the pounding. Mr. Bezruchenko, a few paragraphs down, there is a paragraph beginning with: "Hoxha said three civilians." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: This refers to a NLA Commander Hoxha. It says that: "Hoxha said three civilians had been killed in the combat but the army denied there are any left, i.e., there are any civilians left after a mass exodus provoked by the NLA's entry into the suburb two weeks ago." Does this information indicate that it was at least reported that there were disputes regarding casualties that occurred at Aracinovo, whether they be civilian or otherwise?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It indeed does, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Earlier, Mr. Bezruchenko, you mentioned that -- or excuse me, I should say on cross-examination, you mentioned that the withdrawal of the NLA forces from Aracinovo occurred in NATO vehicles. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did this NLA withdrawal occur in a disciplined manner, according to your research?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What significance, if anything -- what was the significance, if any, of that disciplined withdrawal for your assessment of NLA capabilities?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is obvious from this particular instance that NLA clearly enjoyed the level of discipline which made it possible for the NLA to carry out tactical actions, including the action of withdrawal.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would seek to tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As exhibit P495, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'd like you, please, to turn your mind, Mr. Bezruchenko, to the month of August 2001. My colleague asked you several questions about the events of that month. And specifically at pages 7122 to 7126 of the transcript on the 1st of November, you were asked about the casualties suffered by members of the Macedonian security forces in August 2001. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bezruchenko, is the intensity of an armed conflict only measured in the numbers -- or numbers of casualties?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not really.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we show the witness, please, what is Prosecution 65 ter number 215. Your Honours, this document is dated the 12th of August, 2001. It was provided to the Office of the Prosecutor by Goran Mitevski, who, in 2001 was the head of the public security bureau of the Ministry of the Interior. And it's titled an information. It's from operative action Ramno headquarters, information on events and data received at the headquarters of operative action Ramno, in relation to the current situation in the Republic of Macedonia in the period between 0700 and 1500 hours on 12 August 2001. If we can focus, please, on the last paragraph of this page. And if we could enlarge that last paragraph, I would be very grateful.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bezruchenko, the Ramno headquarters received information that -- received information from OVR Karpos that fighting between the Macedonian security forces and the Albanian terrorist groups in the area of the village of Radusa intensified yet again at around 0500 hours, with the security forces of the army of the Republic of Macedonia using Howitzers and a tank at around 0600 hours at the place called Ramniste while infantry forces with some vehicles were clearing the terrain along the main road. Have you followed me?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You may have described this during your direct examination, but it seems like a long time ago now. What is a Howitzer?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Howitzer is a piece of artillery of a calibre which may range between 120 and 200-plus millimetres which normally had a specific trajectory of fire and normally could be used as well as to destroy the enemy manpower in open field as well as to destroy heavy fortifications, like bunkers, fortified houses and the like.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Militarily what is the significance of using Howitzers and a tank against an opposing force, along with infantry?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would suggest to me that the Macedonian forces were actually trying to dislodge the NLA from the area that the NLA was holding in -- by infantry attacks supported by tanks and artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Would the kinds of weaponry used by an army be relevant to the intensity of an armed conflict to evaluating the intensity of an armed conflict?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, this is a major indicator.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: How about occupation of public facilities by one side to the armed conflict that would be another indication?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it definitely would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we can turn to the next page of this document, please. And if we can focus there on the middle of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You see there's a paragraph, Mr. Bezruchenko, that begins with the phrase: "The shooting." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And in the middle of that paragraph we see: "At around 1200 hours, following a telephone call from SVR Tetovo, two larger groups of Albanian terrorists were observed; one group of 50 to 60 terrorists at the Kiril and Metodi primary school and five groups of approximately 50 Albanian terrorists at the agricultural college who did not engage in any activities and merely paraded around." Are you with me?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What about cutting off important communication lines or the cutting of important communication links?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I see my colleague is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, simply to indicate that we appear to witness a further examination-in-chief, Your Honour. We haven't intervened on the previous question because the document was there and it may be of assistance to the Chamber but those issues, the occupation, as called by my colleague, of civilian facilities and the cutting of communication links were not issues, as I recall, that were raised during the cross-examination. I think to the extent they would have been relevant, they should have been raised by my colleague during the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, what was raised during cross-examination was the issue of the levels or number of casualties that occurred amongst Macedonian security forces during the month in August. And the clear implication of that line of questioning was that the level -- since the level of casualties was low, then there would not have been an armed conflict taking place during that month. And so what I want to continue exploring with this witness is what are, in addition to numbers of casualties, other indicators of the existence of an armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Carry on, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bezruchenko, would the cutting of important communication lines by one belligerent party or another be an indication, possible indication, of an armed conflict?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we focus, please, on the very last full sentence on this page, beginning with "in the period."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you see that, Mr. Bezruchenko?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That sentence says: "In the period between 0630 and 1100 hours the Tetovo-to-Skopje main road was closed to traffic in both directions." Can we focus now what is on the first paragraph on this page, please. Because on that first paragraph there is a discussion of two wounded persons, two casualties. It says the following: "The following were admitted to the Tetovo medical centre during the armed clashes on the night of 11 August between the Albanian terrorist groups and the Macedonian security forces in the area of SVR Tetovo." The first we see Ismaili Lika from Tetovo, and his address, with a gun-shot wound. And then we see Acevski, Vladimir, also from Tetovo, age 1949 -- born in 1949, who was hit in the chest by shrapnel near the sports centre. Do you see that, Mr. Bezruchenko?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm actually going out of order and I apologise. I'm going to come back to this later. Would you recall on Friday -- would you recall that last Friday, Mr. Bezruchenko, at page 71 -- I see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Apostolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise to my colleague Daniel Saxon for interrupting him. You mentioned two patients, Ismail Lika and Acevski, Vladimir. Would it be fair to ask an additional question to him whether they were members of the Macedonian security forces or civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think that was coming. Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bezruchenko, does the document in front of you indicate whether the two gentlemen mentioned are civilians, members of the Macedonian security forces, or members of the NLA? Is there any indication there?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The way I'm reading this document and I think this is -- there is a sufficient indication to suggest that these two individuals were both civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we can leave this -- well, no, I won't leave this right now. If we can turn, please, to what is Exhibit P393. Briefly. Your Honours, to save time, this is the -- actually, I am -- I apologise. I'm in the wrong document. If we could please show the witness what is known as the Ministry of Interior's "White Book."

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: It is Exhibit P45, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bezruchenko, do you recall using this document, this book, as one of the sources of your report?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And do you recall that this so-called "White Book" contains the lists of civilians, police and army soldiers who were killed or injured during the conflict in 2001?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to speed things up, the Prosecution will make an offer of proof that the names of neither gentlemen that we saw a moment ago on our screen, Lika Ismaili, Vladomir Acevski, are found on the lists contained in the "White Book."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bezruchenko, if we can now go back to what is 65 ter 215, please. And if we could go to the second page of the document. And if we could focus on the second full paragraph, beginning with: "The following." Mr. Bezruchenko, just one more question about these two injured persons. If the names of these two casualties or injured or wounded persons is not found in the Ministry of Interior's "White Book", in their lists of casualties, would that be an indication that these lists of casualties could be incomplete?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that indeed would be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: A few moments ago you said that the cutting of important communication lines could be an indication of the existence of an armed conflict. On page 7180 of the transcript last Friday, Mr. Apostolski asked you to confirm whether, in 2001, the NLA had no railway station under its control and you responded to the best of your knowledge, not under physical control. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we can turn now to what is exhibit 393, please, P393, which is the annual report of the Ministry of the Interior for 2001. And if we can look at the English -- the portion of the English translation that starts at ERN N005-0691. And if we could turn to the fifth page of this English portion. And it's page 83 in the Macedonian version of this report, this annual report. And if we could scroll down to the bottom of the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bezruchenko, there's a paragraph beginning with "the current events in the Republic." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If you look in the middle of this paragraph you see a sentence. It says that: "Because of perpetrated terrorist acts and the presence of armed persons, the railway line Skopje-Kicevo, was interrupted since 23 June 2001." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, before I forget, I would seek to tender Prosecution 65 ter 215. It was the last the document that I showed and reviewed with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As exhibit P496, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bezruchenko, I would like to move to another topic, please. At page 7180 of the transcript, my colleague Mr. Apostolski asked you: "Is it correct that the NLA had no city under its control?" And you responded: "I don't think that the NLA had any cities under its complete control." Do you recall that exchange?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bezruchenko, is Tetovo the second largest city in Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we show the witness, please, what is Exhibit P00481.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bezruchenko, this document was also the topic of discussion during cross-examination at pages 6946 to 6948 of the transcript. And if we could focus -- it is a resolution from the 5th of August, 2001, from then the president Macedonia, Boris Trajkovski. And if we could focus, please, on paragraph 1, President Trajkovski says the following: "The army of the Republic of Macedonia, with necessary structure and force, is to enter the town of Tetovo with the aim of preventing its fall into the hands of the terrorist groups of the self-styled NLA and protecting the lives, safety, and property of the citizens of Tetovo." Mr. Bezruchenko, what was going on in the city of Tetovo during the first part of August 2001?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation in and around Tetovo was extremely tense. The city was under almost daily shelling. The number of security casualties as well as a number of civilian casualties was still mounting, and parts of the city were actually under NLA control. Fighting was going on in some parts of the city, street fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we show the witness, please, what is Exhibit 1D00229. Your Honour, this document was originally written in German. These are intelligence reports written by members of the government of Germany who were working in Macedonia during the summer of 2001. And if we can turn to what is page 10 in the English version and it's also page 10 in the Macedonian version. And if we could focus on the two paragraphs underneath the date: Skopje, 9 August 2001. No, I want to go back to the next -- excuse me, please go back to the previous page in English. No, something has -- if we can back one more page in English, please. Thank you. And if we could focus on the bottom half of this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bezruchenko, this was a report written on the 9th of August, 2001. And the report tells us the following: "The situation in the area of Tetovo is deteriorating considerably. As before, the town of Tetovo is predominantly under the control of the NLA." Next sentence: "Since about 1700 hour, serious battles have again been developing in and around Tetovo. Heavy weapons such as mortars and artillery (only the Macedonian military forces) have been deployed on both sides. The NLA seems to be concentrated at the Kuzman barracks," and then in the last sentence: "Furthermore the continued use of a Mi-24 weapons system has been reported." Mr. Bezruchenko what is an Mi-24 weapons system?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is in fact gun ship, helicopter, combat helicopter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The next paragraph begins: "In the morning, around 1000 to 1130 hours there was a gun fight. (Hand-held weapons and hand grenades used) between the Macedonian military forces and the NLA in the northerly part of the centre of Tetovo." And then lower down in that paragraph we see: "The few Slavic Macedonian inhabitants who had stayed in Tetovo are now beginning generally to leave Tetovo in order to find shelter with relatives or friends in Skopje. According to so far unconfirmed reports, significant parts of the Macedonian security forces also left the town in the afternoon." Have you followed that with me, Mr. Bezruchenko?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we go to the very next page, please. And can we look at the top of the page, please. And we see that there was a conversation with the acting commander of the 112th NLA Brigade and the first paragraph begins with the following sentence: "The acting commander of the 112th NLA Brigade reports that his mission was now been accomplished." Did the 112th NLA Brigade operate in the Tetovo area?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bezruchenko, what does this document tell us from a military perspective about the success of the Macedonian security forces's efforts to enter Tetovo and prevent it from falling into the hands of the NLA as had been ordered by the president on the 5th of August?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document suggests that there was fierce fighting going on in the city, that significant parts of the city were in fact under NLA control, and that the Macedonian security forces apparently failed to carry out the mission, to drive the NLA out of the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, would this be a convenient time to take the first break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. We will adjourn now and resume a little after quarter past.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, on the screen in front of you is the last document that I reviewed with the witness. It is actually MFI 1D00-229, but rather than seeking to tender this document, I have learned during the break the Prosecution's 65 ter exhibit 284, actually is slightly more comprehensive than what has been MFI'd as 1D00-229. If we could show the witness, please, what is 65 ter number 284. That is not -- yes, it is. Can we see the next English translation portion of this document, please. Can we go -- this 65 ter exhibit has been -- has about four or five English portions to it, and one of them is 43 pages long. Yes. Your Honour, this is the start of the last group of intelligence reports that I reviewed with Mr. Bezruchenko before the break. If we can please now look at the English translation for the ERN range N001-8764 to 8780. And, Your Honours, this particular ERN range is not within what has been marked for identification as 1D00-229. And if we could turn to the 11th page within this range, please. And this range, Your Honours, is a compilation of information about many members of the National Liberation Army in 2001. And if we could perhaps enlarge the bottom paragraph on this page. It's about a man known as Cela, the commander of the 112th Brigade, and perhaps if we could make this into a single page so that we could read that entire paragraph. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bezruchenko, we see, for example, that on this page there is a description of the this man known as Cela, commander or high ranking position in the staff of the 112th Brigade. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And we see that he has close cooperation with the 115th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And his area of responsibility is believed to be west of the General Djankovic border crossing, Skopje, as well as the operations zones of Tetovo, Gostivar, and Debar. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters have difficulties hearing the counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If this person was a commander or high-ranking position of the staff of the 112th Brigade with the area of responsibility including Tetovo, would this person have had some responsibility for the NLA units fighting in Tetovo that we saw earlier in this document?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I would seek to tender what is 65 ter 284.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that at the time when we had sought to tender the previous document which had been MFI'd as Exhibit 1D229 there was an objection by the Prosecutor based on the size of the document and in particular based on the fact that only certain parts of documents had been used at the time and the agreement, as I understand it - in any case, what matters - the ruling of the Chamber at the time was to the effect that only those parts which have been used would be tendered and the agreement, if I may call that, at the time was for this document to continue to be used during the trial and those part which have been used with particular witness to be sought to be tendered at the end. I believe that the same principle should apply to this particular document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I apologise if there was agreement that I was not aware of. Is the understanding of that agreement that there would be no tendering of this exhibit until the close of the Prosecution case?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I don't want to mislead Mr. Saxon with my terms but I remember the objection of the Prosecution to the effect that the document should not be tendered as a whole because only certain parts of the documents had been shown and the Chamber, as I understood and as I seem to remember, accepted the Prosecution submissions on that point. And the Defence propose to MFI the document and indicated at that time that it would seek to tender those parts of the documents which would have been used by the end of the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, perhaps it would be appropriate, then, if the-- well, in the Prosecution's submission, at this point it would be appropriate to tender the entire document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And how is the document supported by oral evidence of this witness? He has dealt with one or two isolated pages in what you mention is a very large document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, that -- that is true, Your Honour. However, by dealing with those pages he has, in the Prosecution's submission, established the relevance certainly of at least part of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. That's where we were along time ago --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- with the Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. I did not make the objection that was made before. And I -- I apologise if the Prosecution has created confusion. But if the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Not confusion; a system which I think we will adhere to. So I'd suggest that and Mr. Mettraux need to talk about which pages of this material have been dealt with in the course of evidence and which you think need now to be put before the Chamber, in addition to what we may be revealed by the actual transcript of the questioning concerning those pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bezruchenko, you were asked during cross-examination whether the NLA had barracks, and you answered that, no, to your knowledge, the NLA did not have barracks. Do you recall that exchange?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If an army enjoys the support of the local population, does it need barracks to survive?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not really.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we show what is Prosecution 65 ter 926, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That may be a wrong reference. There's no such document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Then I will move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can -- Mr. Bezruchenko, can a brigade headquarters function as a barracks?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would not be an unusual situation, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we show the witness what is Exhibit P493, please. Again, this is a document compiled by NATO in September of 2001. And if we can turn to page 16 of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bezruchenko, this is a photograph of the brigade headquarters of the 113th Brigade in the village of Lipkovo, and we see a reference -- there's a line pointed to a spot that's referred to as Sokoli's office. Do you know who Sokoli was?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was the alias of one of the NLA commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Could members of the NLA sleep in a building like that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they could.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right, Yesterday at pages 7293 to 7294 my colleague Mr. Apostolski asked you about evidence or documents indicating that the NLA maintained training centres, and Mr. Apostolski showed you Exhibit P485, a document that had been produced by the intelligence sector of the Macedonian Ministry of Defence, and my colleague asked you whether you had seen other documents which described NLA training centres other than the document shown to you yesterday. Do you recall that exchange?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we show, once again, what has been marked for identification as Exhibit 1D229. And if we could turn to page 34 in the English version. And can we move forward one page, please. Can we move forward one page again, please. And if we focus on the last half of that page --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You see -- you see there's a paragraph beginning with the phrase: "According to." Do you see that, Mr. Bezruchenko.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It says that: "According to mutually independent reports from a Macedonian Slavic source and an Albanian source, a training camp for irregulars has been discovered in Kosovo in the area of Globocica." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And down below that, we see the assumed camp has until recently been used for military purposes but the extent of activity cannot accurately -- cannot be accurately determined. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we turn to the next page, please. We see references to sleeping pads, blankets, pillows, et cetera, cooking facilities. And if we scroll up there's a discussion about other things that were found in the area, such as medical equipment, fox hole, grocery crates and then under the phrase, Preliminary assessment, we see: "Fresh truck tracks as well as a condition of evidence and blankets found in the camp indicate (under consideration of the weather conditions over the last few days) that the facility has been in use until just recently." Do you see that, Mr. Bezruchenko?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Militarily, why would it be logical for the NLA to have established training camps within Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be logical because such a training camp would not be within the reach of the Macedonian security forces, meaning that they would not be in a position to raid this camp or to shell it with artillery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Simply to indicate, in our view at the least, the question by Mr. Saxon was suggestive to the extent that it suggested that the camp in question was a camp of the NLA. I believe that's not what the text says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'll move on to another topic, Mr. Bezruchenko. During cross-examination, you were asked a number of questions related to NLA regulations. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And you mentioned that you thought that some regulations might have been taken from the regulations of the Kosovo Protection Corps or other army manuals. Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bezruchenko, do you have any idea how many armies around the world have taken or borrowed manuals or portions of manuals from other more established armies?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is really difficult to say, but I would imagine that this could be quite a significant number.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bezruchenko, are you familiar with the manual of the army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am, with some of them, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And do you know whether parts of that army's manuals were taken from another army's manual or manuals?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Which army manual was the source for the army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Normally that was a manual of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the manual or manuals of the army of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you know whether parts of this manual or manuals were taken from another army's manual?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Which army manual was the source for the army of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those which I saw were also derived from the sources within the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bezruchenko, when you started your military career, were you an officer of the army of the Soviet Union?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And were you then -- did you become familiar with the army manuals of the army of the Republic of -- excuse me, the army of the Soviet Union?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: After the breakup of the Soviet Union, did you become an officer in the army of the Republic of the Ukraine?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And during that time in your career, did you become familiar with manuals of the army of Ukraine?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Are there any similarities between the manual of the army of the Republic of Ukraine and the manual or manuals of the army of the USSR?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is quite a number of those, particularly in relation to internal regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Bezruchenko, during cross-examination you were asked about crimes that were committed during the conflict and crimes committed by the NLA. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You are now a citizen of the Ukraine. Is that right.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Are you familiar then with the history of the German army's operations and activities in the Ukraine during the Second World War?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did the German army commit crimes in the Ukraine during the Second World War?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No doubt, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: In your opinion as a military professional, was the German army still an army, even though its members committed some crimes?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it was indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you, please, to turn your mind to the events in Ljuboten in August 2001. Mr. Tarculovski -- excuse me, Mr. Apostolski asked you on cross-examination if you had seen any document that described a police unit commanded by Johan Tarculovski that went into Ljuboten. Do you recall that exchange?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we please show the witness what is part of Exhibit P379, marked for identification, and if it helps the court officer, it is also Prosecution 65 ter document 285.24. It's a document with the ERN range N000-8957 to N000-8959.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bezruchenko, this is a report dated the 6th of May, 2003. It's a report of the meeting of the commission of the Ministry of Interior investigating the events in Ljuboten village.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we scroll down, please, so we can see the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bezruchenko, the first sentence of the last paragraph says that: "Johan Tarculovski played the main role in the combat operations in Ljuboten village ..." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. There's a reference then to Mr. Boskoski.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if we can turn to the following page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And at the first paragraph of this page, we see a sentence that says: "Tarculovski and the rest of the reservists were issued weapons (semi-automatic rifles and pistols) at the centre for the education of security personnel at the order of the then minister ..." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if you look at the next paragraph, in the middle of the paragraph we see: "In order to achieve this goal, between 10 and 12 August 2001, Tarculovski, who knew the area well, first entered the village in the early morning hours with around 20 people, ten of whom were from Kometa and the rest were reservists." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if you could just look briefly, please, at the last paragraph, there is a sentence in the middle that says: "Meanwhile, meanwhile, the population was slowly leaving the village and Tarculovski and his team as well as the other 80 men entered several houses." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you review this document as part of the preparation for your report?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And did this document factor into your analysis of whether Mr. Tarculovski led a unit of policemen into Ljuboten village?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we please show the witness what is within -- I see my colleague on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Apostolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... Your Honour, for interfering with your cross-examination, but when I asked my question of the witness Bezruchenko it was whether he had seen a text quoting that it was police units of Johan Tarculovski. I quote: "Police unit of Johan Tarculovski."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Carry on, please, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we please show the witness another document from this same MFI 379. It has Prosecution 65 ter number 285.13. It has ERN number N000-8927.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bezruchenko, this is an Official Note drafted by the head of the sector for internal affairs at Cair in 2001. There's a typo in the date on this document. It should say 19 November 2003.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we turn to the next page, please, in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
