utterances.text: Mr. Bezruchenko, if you look towards the bottom -- the second half of that long paragraph, you see there's a sentence beginning with: "On the 11th, around 1500 hours." It is now in the middle of the page. Do you see it?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That sentence says: "On the 11th, around 1500 hours, some people in police uniforms arrived at the grounds of police station Cair, about whom I later learned that they are reservists from, of the minister of internal affairs." A few lines below that there is a sentence that begins with: "Around 20 minutes later." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: "Around 20 minutes later the person Johan came and requested transportation for his policemen to the community centre in village Ljubanci." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we turn, please, to what is page 4 of the English version of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bezruchenko, about five lines down from the top, there is a sentence that says: "While the minister was there." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: "While the minister was there, Johan's group was bringing around 10 captured Albanians from village." Did you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if you look down that paragraph, there is -- about five lines up from the bottom of that paragraph, there's a phrase in the middle that says: "After 1430 hours." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And that sentence says: "After 1430 hours, all persons from the unit that was led by Johan left with their (illegible) from village Ljuboten." Mr. Bezruchenko, was this one of the documents that you reviewed in the preparation of your report?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And was this one of the documents that led you to refer to the police unit led by Mr. Tarculovski?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Apostolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours, for interruption. Could the witness please state, or if the counsel can ask the witness in which footnote of his report he used this information, if he used it at all.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure if I can tell you exactly which footnote it was, but I definitely have seen this document and I reviewed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bezruchenko, at page 6986 of the transcript, my colleague Mr. Mettraux asked you whether you agreed that the Ljuboten matter was dealt with at "the president and command level." Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we please show the witness what is Exhibit P402, please. And if we could turn, please, to the portion of the English translation that begins with ERN number N000-9695. In the Macedonian version, it would be page 53.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Bezruchenko, I made a mistake a moment ago. I described to you a question from Mr. Mettraux, but I didn't complete it. It was that whether you agreed that the Ljuboten matter was dealt with at the president and command level but not within the Ministry of Interior. That was the question. And in this section of Mr. Boskoski's book, My Battle for Macedonia, can we scroll down, please, to the bottom paragraph that begins: On August 10th." And you see, Mr. Bezruchenko, that that paragraph begins with the terrorist ambush at Ljubotenski Bacila. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It describes how eight members of the army of Macedonia were killed. And then it says the following: "The Ministry of Internal Affairs and the Ministry of Defence undertook a joint operation to break up the terrorist group which operated in that area." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And then a few lines down it talks about the armed clashes of the joint security forces of the Republic of Macedonia conducted on August 11 and 12 in Ljuboten village. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What, if anything, does this tell you about whether the Ljuboten matter, so to speak, was dealt with within the Ministry of the Interior or not?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: My assessment would be that this matter was dealt with at the highest level of the Ministry of Interior and it was dealt with in cooperation with the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we please show the witness what is Exhibit P0073, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bezruchenko, this is a decision signed by Ljube Boskoski to establish a commission to consider the circumstances and analyse the activities undertaken by the security forces of the Ministry of Internal Affairs to repel the armed attacks by terrorist groups on 12 August 2001 in the village of Ljuboten, Skopje. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if you go, please, to what -- the paragraph that is at Roman numeral II and we see in the middle of that paragraph it says: "The commission from item 1 of this decision, has the task to review the circumstances and analyse the activities undertaken by the security forces of the Ministry of Internal Affairs to repel the armed attacks of terrorist groups on 12 August 2001 in the village of Ljuboten, Skopje." What, if anything, does this language tell us about whether the Ljuboten matter was dealt with within the Ministry of Interior or not?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apparently the Ljuboten matter was dealt with at the level of the Ministry of Interior, and it is also obvious that a special commission was formed on the orders of the minister to look into the circumstances of this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You'll be pleased, I'm sure, Mr. Bezruchenko, to know that that concludes the questions to be asked of you. It has been, in our experience, a record, and we would like to thank you for the time that you have spent and the assistance that you have given. The court officer will now assist you and you will be able to leave the courtroom, and return to your ordinary affairs. Thank you indeed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much Your Honours. It was a pleasure for me as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Before we move on, can I indicate that the Chamber held its hand during the questioning of this witness because it realised, in particular, the significance that could be attached to his evidence and that therefore it was proper that both Defence counsel have full opportunity to cross-examine, and we realised also that there was an issue concerning the independence of the witness because of his role in the Office of the Prosecutor. Even so, can I indicate, in the view of the Chamber, the cross-examination, in particular, was extremely long and unnecessarily so, and we say that to make it very clear that the Chamber will not be so quiet should there be an attempt to cross-examine other witnesses in such detail and so extensively. I think the Chamber has made it clear, although it really should not need to make it clear, that there are issues that are of importance in this case and there are many other issues, and it is certainly not going to advance the full and fair and proper adjudication of this case to spend a great deal of time on issues that are of little or no significance to the ultimate matters of importance. Having got that off the Chamber's chest, and I now understand that are matters that counsel wish to raise before the next witness is called.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, and we will start by indicating that we will take on board the indication just given by the Chamber and try to accelerate the matter of cross-examination with the remaining witnesses. Your Honour, there are two matters which the Defence of Mr. Boskoski would like to bring the attention of the Chamber at this stage. The first one relates to the proposed evidence of Mr. Ostreni, the next witness; the second issue pertains to an issue of disclosure. Starting with the issue pertaining to Mr. Ostreni, Your Honour, I would simply give a short background which may illuminate the submissions of the Defence. Your Honour will be aware from the evidence at trial that the Macedonian judicial authorities and the Office of the Prosecutor in the course of 2001 and 2002 had collaborated in relation to the investigation of a number of cases. One of those cases, Your Honour may recall, is known as the NLA leadership case. In January of 2002, the Macedonian prosecuting authority had sent information to the Office of the Prosecutor of this Tribunal about this particular case, together with a suggestion, on their part, that this should be one of the cases that the Office of the Prosecutor should take over. This case related, inter alia, to Mr. Gzim Ostreni, the next witness. In May of 2002, the OTP gave notice to the authority that it would take over a number of cases, including the Ljuboten case but also the so-called NLA leadership case. In the course of the same year, 2002, the Prosecution reiterated its request to the national authority to stop any investigation that was going on in relation to the so-called NLA leadership case. In September 2002 the Prosecution formally sought the deferral of five cases, including this case, the NLA leadership case. The Prosecution did not indict any person in relation to the NLA leadership case nor, as far as disclosure suggests, has any formally investigation ever been opened against any individuals relevant to that case. In fact, the Prosecution waited until after the indictment deadline of 31st of December of 2004 before interviewing members of the NLA in the form of statement taken by the OTP. Importantly for these proceedings, Your Honour, the taking over by the Office of the Prosecutor of this particular case, the NLA leadership case, has effectively denied, we submit, the local authorities an opportunity to investigate this matter and has resulted in frustrating any possible investigative effort at national level. More importantly for these proceedings, the actions of the Office of the Prosecutor have in fact denied by a knock-on effect the Defence of Mr. Boskoski an opportunity to obtain any material as might have been elicited by a local investigation. As indicated to Your Honour, the Office of the Prosecutor has only conducted what can be characterised as a very superficial investigation of the NLA and in particular has not conducted what we would consider a formal investigation into the role or involvement of any particular individual --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm very sorry to interrupt. I'm not objecting to the arguments that my colleague is making. However, I would ask that we move into private session because the contents of the arguments touch on what are effectively operational matters of the Office of the Prosecutor, work that was done or not and, in the Prosecution's submission, should not be discussed or described in public session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is this current matters? Or are we talking of past history, Mr. Saxon?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Past history, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps to be as brief as possible and to summarize this particular point, we believe the absence of an investigation in earnest of the role and involvement of particular individuals, members of the NLA into the events which are relevant to these charges as well as the prohibition, to call it that, or the ban made on the local authorities to investigate this matter have had the effect of denying the Defence material that would or could have been relevant to the cross-examination of this particular witness as well as a prior witness, also a member of the NLA. Your Honour, the NLA is a secretive and, we submit, dangerous organisation. We say so, Your Honour, to underline the fact that our ability to investigate the internal functioning of the NLA and to investigate also the involvement of particular witnesses which appear on behalf of the Prosecution as member of the NLA is, to say the least, extremely complicated. In all such --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters kindly request if the counsel can continue at a slower pace. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I apologise and I will attempt to do so. Your Honour, to a large extent, the Defence relies heavily on the investigation which has been conducted by the Office of the Prosecutor and upon the material which the Defence receives as a result of these investigations. In other words, a full and fair investigations of matters and issues relevant to the case by the Office of the Prosecutor is critical to the ability, in turn, of the Defence to exercise its rights and obligations effectively. The Prosecution has notified the Defence and the Trial Chamber recently that it would ask the Chamber to warn the witness that the evidence which he might give in this courtroom could incriminate him. In our view, Your Honour, this request is not only futile but it's also improper. It is futile, in our view, because the Tribunal has no power to give any guarantee to Mr. Ostreni that he will not be prosecuted back in Macedonia and that the record of these proceedings could not be used against him. It is also improper, in our view, Your Honour, because the only thing that has stood between an investigation of the conduct of Mr. Ostreni since at least September of 2002 is the fact that the Prosecution has kept to its chest the investigative material or in any case, the case that pertains to this witness. In effect, the Prosecution is asking the Chamber to warn the Prosecution witness that the Prosecution could at any stage release the case back to the local authorities after relying upon his evidence as a witness of truth against Mr. Boskoski. Our view, Your Honour, it is the Prosecution and not the Chamber which should take the responsibility for this matter which in itself, in our submission, Your Honour, could constitute an abuse of the process. At Nuremberg, Your Honour, to take a example of the past, the Prosecution had to take some very difficult about the way to run its case. One of these tough decision was the decision taken by the Prosecution at the time not to rely on the evidence of accused person against some of their co-defendants. The reason for that decision, Your Honour, was to protect the integrity of the proceedings and the integrity of the record on which the judgment would be based and the judgment of history would be based. The Prosecution at Nuremberg did not seek the assistance of the Chamber, or the Tribunal as it was known at the time, to take those tough decisions. The Prosecution in this case has taken the decision to call as witnesses of truth two members of the NLA, and it is not for Defence to pass judgment on this decision of the Prosecution. However, it is our view that the Prosecution should bear the full consequences of its decision that the responsibility to warn the witness should have been its own and also, we believe, Your Honour, that the Prosecution should accept the evidence of this witness as it will be given as a whole and not to seek later to cherry pick the evidence of the witness. There is another matter, Your Honour, which is directly relevant -- or two other matters which we believe are relevant to the evidence of this proposed witness. The first one relates to a number of documents which relate directly or indirectly to the activities or the structure of the NLA, some of which have been shown to the witness during proofing. During proofing, the proposed witness has given a number of indications about these documents, and in relation to a number of them he has given an indication to the Prosecution that this material, at least some of it, may not be accurate or may be unreliable. It is the view of the Defence that it would be for the Prosecution to the extent that it intends to rely on this document to bring this matter to Your Honour's attention. The Defence does not intend to cross-examine on each of those documents, in particular or in particular one document which is a NATO package which Your Honour has already seen which was prepared, in part, by Mr. Hutsch and which has been shown by Mr. Ostreni and by other personalities to be unreliable in part. Your Honour, there is also, in our view, a fundamental issue of fairness or at least of appearance of fairness. There is a very real issue as far as these proceedings are concerned of a perception that these proceedings are being unfair in a way, to the accused, because one side of the crisis is now being called to give evidence against the people that were facing them on the other side. To this issue of appearance of unfairness, Your Honour, is added the very real fact, as we indicated, that the conduct of these people, the persons, members of the NLA, was never fully investigated by the Office of the Prosecutor, as we indicated, thereby denying the Defence material which would have been directly relevant to its ability to conduct these proceedings and this, we say, creates a very real unfairness. Your Honour, we bring those matters to your attention so that they may be taken into account if Your Honour consider them relevant to assessing the weight, if any, to be given to the evidence of Mr. Ostreni and Mr. Bushi at the end of this case. We also wished to bring them to Your Honour's attention to make it clear that is the Defence position that the evidence of Mr. Ostreni should be considered as a whole, whether it is reliable or not, and that the Prosecution having taken the decision to call that witness should accept him as it is, as he is, and not seek at the end of the case to cherry pick within the evidence of that witness. And perhaps, Your Honour, if permitted, I will turn to the second issue, which, unfortunately, is not much of a good news, either. Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is it related or quite different?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: It is quite different, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think we might deal with this matter, if anything further is to be said on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Apostolski, is there anything you wish to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to support my learned colleague Mr. Mettraux and I would like to give some brief additions. In the beginning, I wouldn't like to attack anybody from the Prosecutor's office, but I would like to point out some things. The Defence of Mr. Johan Tarculovski, ever since its beginnings when the indictment against Boskoski and Tarculovski was published, the Defence was very upset because this -- the Prosecution of this Tribunal decided not to prosecute the leaders of the so-called NLA. Your Honours, this is a historical event for the Republic of Macedonia and this Tribunal is perceived as an instrument that is supposed to contribute to the peace and conciliation in the Republic of Macedonia. The Republic of Macedonia is the only republic of former Yugoslavia which won its independence without a war and sufferings. It was the only former Yugoslav republic that decided to respond to all provocations and all problems with tolerance, both within the country and outside. The Defence of Johan Tarculovski is even more upset when it found out that the leaders of the so-called NLA are witnesses. Maybe the Defence is not experienced enough to understand how can people that are responsible for all sufferings in the Republic of Macedonia in 2001 be called as witnesses in a process against international criminal law and to be expected to give sincere testimonies that would corroborate the positions of the Prosecutor and that there was conflict war in -- in Macedonia and that the goal of NLA was to fight for more rights and for alleged discrimination against Albanian population, which are the thesis of the Prosecutor's which they accepted blindly by believing the leaders of the so-called NLA. Your Honours, we attorneys were taught even ever since in the faculty of law that the main principle is that everybody is equal before the law. In Macedonia and any other criminal law, everybody is equal before the law and is accountable for the crime that is a crime according to the law, and in all criminal laws it is not allowed to the Prosecution to select what are the persons that should be brought to justice for their crimes and who should not. Everybody should be responsible for the crimes they have committed. Your Honours, these people should be sitting in this Tribunal but as accused and to be found responsible for all crimes that they have committed in the Republic of Macedonia and against Macedonians responsible for the ethnic cleansings, ethnic cleansing of Macedonian minorities in areas where there are 7.000 Macedonians, in areas where people have not yet returned to their homes because members of NLA burned their houses, they kidnapped their husbands and fathers, or their mothers. The only scene of home was their ethnicity. They should be tried for all rapes of innocent construction workers, murders and kidnappings of civilians, execution of innocent people, and in general for bringing the term "mass graves" into Macedonia. Your Honours, through calling them as witnesses, the Prosecutor's office is walking on thin ice, as introducing a principle in the international humanitarian law which will provide legitimacy and amnesty to any perpetrator of crime if they only choose the site that the Prosecutor's Office considers should not be held responsible for the crimes that they have committed. Your Honours, in this way amnestied are the persons who are the most responsible for bringing the terrorism into the so-called peace oasis, as everyone used to call the Republic of Macedonia. The most puzzling is the notion of the Prosecutor's office failing to investigate the crimes for which the NLA leaders are responsible. Although they had more than four years, since without learning of the facts, they decided, a priori, that these people should not be held responsible and by this they introduced a legal and historical distortion about the truth about 2001 but also the future of the international law. By taking the case, the NLA leadership, the Prosecutor's office, in a way, put on a shelf the crimes perpetrated by these people, not allowing the authorities in the Republic of Macedonia the possibility to investigate all these crimes and, a priori, provided them amnesty without any supporting arguments. This has denied the Defence the opportunity to be fully prepared to cross-examine these witnesses and to prepare quality Defence for their clients, which is guaranteed with the right to fair trial. And why has the Prosecutor's office of this Honourable Tribunal to give, a priori, amnesty to these persons without conducting an investigation, the history will show, and I hope that the international criminal law will point the finger to this notion, how justice should not be selected in advance. I thank this Honourable Tribunal for the opportunity to speak as the Defence counsel of Mr. Johan Tarculovski and also the only Macedonian representing in this Tribunal. And I hope that this honourable tribunal will take my words into account when it will decide on the weight given to the testimony and evidence of Mr. Ostreni and Mr. Nazim Bushi. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Apostolski. Is there anything you wish to say, Mr. Saxon?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Preliminarily, Your Honour, Your Honours, the Prosecution believes that it is the Defence who, at this moment are walking on thin legal ice, rather than the Prosecution. The Prosecution suggests that if the tables were turned and we were in the Defence case and prior to the commencement of the testimony of a Defence witness, Prosecution stood up and made submissions to the Chamber suggesting that a Defence witness should be sitting in the dock in this Tribunal or is in any other way not fit to be a witness, then the Prosecution predicts that such a submission would meet with a very quick and probably strong response, both from the Defence, and from the Trial Chamber. Secondly, Your Honours, the Defence contends that they are somehow prejudiced because the cases related to the members of the NLA were deferred to the Office of the Prosecutor. But that's not the case, Your Honour. The Prosecution, in this case, has disclosed, for example, just in one particular disclosure between five and 6.000 pages of court files, testimony, eye-witness testimony, victim witness testimony related to alleged crimes committed by members of the NLA. The Prosecution, in its investigations into the so-called NLA cases, interviewed witnesses and took either statements or investigator's notes and that material has been disclosed to the Defence in this case. In no way has the Prosecution "kept to its chest," as my colleague suggests, investigative material that is relevant to this witness. On the contrary. The Prosecution, to the best of its ability has disclosed all material in its knowledge, in its possession that relate to the next witness, Mr. Ostreni. My colleague suggests that a warning pursuant to Rule 90 (E) be futile and an abuse of process. The Prosecution finds this argument to be somewhat strange indeed because frankly, Your Honours, the original suggestion that Mr. Ostreni might need to receive this warning came from counsel for Mr. Tarculovski to the Prosecution. Secondly, Your Honours, it is not futile because the witness, once given a warning, may still choose not to respond to questions that may incriminate him, and although the rule says he may be compelled to answer questions, we all know that there are -- have been witnesses who have refused to answer certain questions, even upon threat of contempt. My colleagues suggest that there is a fundamental issue of fairness at stake here, and they suggest that there is a perception that these proceedings are unfair to the Defence, because "only one side is being called to give evidence." Only one side of the conflict in 2001. But that also is not correct, Your Honours. In this case, the Prosecution has called witnesses from both -- from members of both belligerent parties to the armed conflict in Macedonia in 2001, Members of the NLA, members of the Macedonian police and Ministry of the Interior, members of the Macedonian army. And the Prosecution did so so that the Trial Chamber could hear their evidence, the evidence of all sides and evaluate this evidence. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I don't think so, Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: It was simply a clarification, not a reply, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Chamber has given counsel considerable liberty in what has just been said, because in very many respects the comments offered have not been either directly relevant or proper. This Chamber has the role and responsibility, quite independently of either Prosecution or Defence, or of political considerations, to determine questions of whether an accused person charged before the Chamber is proved to be guilty of any of the offences with which that person is charged. That is the responsibility this Chamber has and it does it without regard to what may be social or political influences and it will do -- continue to perform that role in its conduct of this trial. The submissions have not been to the point of any procedural matter to be dealt with at this point, and if they have relevance in the trial, it is a relevance as to the weight to be attached to evidence, and that is a matter which would normally and properly have been dealt with in the course of closing submissions, when all matters of weight and relevance are considered by this Tribunal. And in so far as any of the matters raised are thought to have substance, they will be taken into account at that time. Was there any other matter that needs to be dealt with before the witness is called? Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Unfortunately, yes, Your Honour, and a brief one, hopefully. We'd simply bring to Your Honour's attention that on 29 and 31st of October of 2007, respectively, the Defence was provided by the Prosecution would two pictures or photos taken from the village of Ljuboten. They are panoramic photos of which Your Honour have already been acquainted with. These picture were received upon a specific request to the Prosecution by the Defence of Mr. Tarculovski, and thanks to the diligence of Mr. Tarculovski, these two pictures, Your Honour, were annotated by two individuals who had been interviewed by the Office of the Prosecution and on those two pictures the two individuals had made annotations of places and location in which they said fire had been directed at the army from inside the village. They have identified specific houses and location. We believe that this renewed failure, Your Honour, of disclose -- to disclose that material is again a particularly serious one, considering that one of the two persons who had prepared one of those drawing was a witness in this case who has appeared a long time ago. It was Witness M-051. We believe that this again is a indication of what starts to become a pattern of failed disclosure of material which clearly is relevant and clearly is exculpatory in nature. We would also bring another fact to Your Honour's attention in relation to these particular witnesses is that both of them were interviewed and the documents obtained, again from the investigator in this case, Mr. Kuehnel, who is to appear as a witness in this case. The Defence believe that once again it is being prejudiced by the late disclosure of this material which should have been in the hands of the Defence at the time when at least M-051 was appearing as a witness and we believe that this pattern, we say, of failed disclosure certainly create impediments for the Defence and do not serve the interests of justice, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Maybe just a little bit more clear, Mr. Mettraux. You're saying that two witnesses who have given evidence here have marked photographs or panoramas during investigation. Is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I apologise. I wasn't clear, Your Honour. Two people were interviewed. There were two interviewees. One of two person appeared as a witness. It was M-051.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I see. Only one, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And the second person --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. And you were not given access to that material--

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Until last week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Anything, Mr. Apostolski? Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Mettraux has provided an accurate description of events. The reason these two photographs were not previously disclosed is because they were marked in the OTP's computer system with what is called a surrogate sheet and what was disclosed to the Defence some years ago were these surrogate sheets describing this material but not the photograph, the annotated photographs themselves. At this time, the Prosecution would not object, if the Defence so desires, to either tendering one or both of these photographs into evidence; or, if the Defence wishes, to have this Witness M-051 recalled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: In the Chamber's view, counsel for the Defence should consider whether either Witness M-051 need be recalled; or whether one or both of the marked panoramas should be admitted into evidence; or, as we understand it, the third option that no further particular action be taken and the matter left where it is and dealt with in the course of final submission. And we would suggest that that should be done in the course of this week, if you could, Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I'm grateful for this indication, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. That being the case, then, we will have the break now and resume after the break at 10 past with the new witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Ostreni.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you take the card that is given to you now and read aloud the affirmation on it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Chamber would mention to you that if, during your evidence, you are asked about a matter that you believe could incriminate you, that is, could amount to some admission of your guilt of an offence or could provide material evidence that you have committed an offence, then it is open to you to say that you do not wish to answer that question. The Chamber is not entirely sure of the position in Macedonia, so we wanted to ensure that you were aware of that matter in the course of giving your own evidence. The other matter the Chamber would mention is that we are sorry that you were so long delayed before you were able to come into court. We had to spend a lot of time with the previous witness and with some other matters. And we are sorry that you were delayed. Now, I believe that Ms. Regue has some questions for you. Ms. Regue.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Thanks, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, General.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: For the record, Your Honour, the Prosecution will call Gzim Ostreni.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: General, do you recall providing a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor in 2005?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Do you recall meeting with a lady from the registry in 2006 who certified your statement?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Do you recall introducing some handwritten changes to your statement at that time?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: For the record, Your Honour, the witness corrected the spelling of his first name in the first page of his statement, and then in paragraph 5, seventh line, he replaced Youth Archery Association by Association for Weapon Training. In the paragraph 6, last line, he replace 1999 by 1991. And in paragraph 34, sixth line, 113th should be replaced by 112th.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: General, have you had the opportunity to read your statement before coming here today?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Are you satisfied that your statement, including the corrections that you introduced, is correct and accurate?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this stage we will seek to tender this witness's statement following Rule 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P497, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: The witness, Gzim Ostreni is a Macedonian citizen of Albanian ethnicity. During 2001, Mr. Ostreni was Chief of General Staff of the NLA. Mr. Ostreni has an extensive military experience which goes back to the early 1960s with the former Yugoslav army. He also graduated from the faculty of philosophy and sociology. Since 1969 he worked with the organs of interior of Macedonia and became chief and later commander of the Territorial Defence. He retired in 1991 with a rank of major. Mr. Ostreni was a member of the KLA from 1999 to 2001 and was actively involved in the military activities in Kosovo. Following the KLA's transformation into the Kosovo Protection Corps, KPC, Mr. Ostreni was promoted to chief of KPC headquarters in March 2000. He had been previously promoted to the rank of general brigadier. Mr. Ostreni subsequently joined the NLA as Chief of Staff in March 2001. He was also known as Plaku. The witness speaks to the discrimination against Albanians and other ethnic minorities in Macedonia prior to 2001. Mr. Ostreni also speaks to the genesis of the NLA and its political goals. He describes the NLA's command structure, including the General Staff, brigades, ranks, manpower, weaponry, equipment, common uniform, finance, logistics as well as operational control. As Chief of Staff, Mr. Ostreni work on the personnel programme, the establishment and organisation of the structural units, staffs and commands as well as the development of internal regulations. The witness also describes the NLA's role in the Ohrid Agreement and Operation Harvest and the official disbandment of the NLA on the 26th, 27th of September, 2001. Your Honours, before we start, we have some binders for the Trial Chamber and also for my learned colleagues and the witness that we can distribute at this stage, I believe. And in the meantime ... In the meantime, we can call 65 ter 778.4, which is tab 4 of the binder. And if you could go to the first page in the Albanian version and the third of the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: General, you may -- you are going to see the document in the screen. But if you wish to see it in paper, you can also look at the binder. I'm going to refer now to tab number 4. I believe that the Albanian version is always the last one in the binder. Tab number 4. Tab 4, yeah.

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI
utterances.text: I found it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Thanks. General, we have in front of us a regulation with a title rules of service of the NLA. We see on the upper left side Ali Ahmeti, and we see on the lower part of the document on the right side your name, General Major Gzim Ostreni. General, did you produce this document?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI
utterances.text: Yes, I worked in the production of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: When did you produce it, approximately?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI
utterances.text: I started in March 2001.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: And when do you believe that you complete it?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI
utterances.text: I tried hard, but I believe that it was completed in end of April.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: In order to produce this document, General, which sources did you use? Which material or knowledge did you rely on?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI
utterances.text: It is rules of service common for all armies. I based myself on the rules of service of the army of the Republic of Albania and bits from the rules of service of the former Yugoslav army and some bits from the Kosovo Protection Corps rules of services.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Your Honour, do you find any problem with the binder?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think you mentioned that it was tab 4.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We found it at tab 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Okay. I'm very sorry, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: As long as we have the right document.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: And it is the case of the three of Your Honours it is tab 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Can I check with my learned colleagues from the Defence if they have also in tab 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Also tab 3. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Maybe we can check if the witness is looking at the right document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tab 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: In fact, Your Honour, I believe what happens is that the English version is under tab 4 and the equivalent to the Albanian is under tab 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Not in ours, Mr. Mettraux, so far. We have both versions in tab 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honours. Maybe at the end of this session, we can review that. I'm terribly sorry. Okay. Can we please go to page 1 of the English translation and also page 2 of the Albanian. It should be, in English, the -- yeah, thanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: General, we see in the upper left side --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. What's on the screen is tab 4.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Yeah, that's what I mean, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, you said in your introductory questions that the witness had signed at the right bottom and Ali Ahmeti was at the left top.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: In the Albanian, because we don't have a cover page of this document in the English version, Your Honour. This document doesn't have a cover page translated into English. So I was looking at the Albanian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can you determine which tab it is we are to look at and which tab it is the witness is speaking about?

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Tab 4, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We better be sure, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: We can check whether the witness is looking at the same document that is on the screen, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: General, in page 2 document that you have, it's the same document that you see on the right side of your screen?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI
utterances.text: Yes, it's the order.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: May I continue, Your Honour? Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: General, if we look at this document we see in the upper left side General Staff, the date, the 2nd of May, 2001, and then we read: "In view of the urgent need to maintain military discipline and professional and moral responsibility in carrying out tasks and on the basis of existing military traditions, I order, that the internal regulations of the NLA, being the fundamental document with regard to establishing and maintaining military discipline as well as reviewing and evaluating disciplinary responsibility, be put into effect." General, which was the purpose of these regulations, of the rules of service of the NLA?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI
utterances.text: In structuring an army, it is of utmost importance to have regulations on basis of which you will establish the hierarchy, who is subordinate to whom and how it will be implemented in practice.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: General, can I take from your answer that with regulation -- with this regulation you were establishing the structure and the hierarchy of the NLA?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI
utterances.text: Yes, and the rules of service of the National Liberation Army itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would submit that there should be very, very careful questioning in relation to this matter and no leading questioning, Your Honour. We believe this was extremely leading as a question.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: General, to whom did you distribute this document once you finished producing it?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI
utterances.text: This document was distributed to all brigade commanders of the NLA.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Had the brigade commanders the obligation to implement these regulations with regards to their subordinates?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI
utterances.text: Yes. This was an obligation stemming from the commander of the National Liberation Army by virtue of this order that I have before me.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Now, if we could look briefly to page 3 of the English where we will see the table of contents.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: General, we see here the table of contents, the first page. In chapter 1, the military oath is mentioned; chapter 2, the flag; chapter 3 the morale betterment and civic education of NLA military personnel; chapter 4, military ceremonies, commemoration and honours; next chapter, the rights and duties of service personnel. Now, if he could go, please, to page 6 of the English translation and page 4 of the Albanian. General we see -- General, you may wish to look at the screen. Maybe it will be easier for you.

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI
utterances.text: Yes, but I didn't have the Albanian document before me. Now I have it.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Maybe the usher can assist the general if he has any problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: General, we see in front of us the military oath. Which significance -- which was the importance of the military oath within the NLA?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI
utterances.text: The military oath is important because when a member makes the oath, certain duties and respect for rights and duties as a military are enumerated to him, and he is reminded of his obligation to abide by the rules of service in the army. He takes the oath and takes upon himself to carry out his duties.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: General, if we look at the second large paragraph of this article with regards to the text of the military oath, we see that in the second line it reads, I quote: "I will always serve to defend and protect the life and property of every citizen of Macedonia. I will always firmly defend human rights and freedoms and in the conduct of my business I will never tolerate discrimination on ethnic, language or allegiance grounds." I end the quote. General, which is the significance of this sentence, in particular the mention to human rights and freedoms when taking the military oath?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI
utterances.text: From our point of view, this was very important, because it is in all documents, in the documents of the United Nations, in the charter of human rights and freedoms and it is of great importance to remind and warn the soldiers and officers of their duty to abide by these rules and not to put into any risk the life of the civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this stage I will seek to tender this regulation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. With a view not to interrupt the flow of the evidence in chief, we give an indication that we will not formally object to any of the NLA documents being admitted. We believe that the issue, if any, of any weight to give to this document may be properly dealt with the Chamber at, as mentioned, the weight stage or the weighing stage of the evidence. We would however indicate that our silence at the point of tendering of any document should not be interpreted as an agreement to the authenticity, reliability or relevance of any of those documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The rules of service at tab 4 will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P498, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: General, you mentioned before that you distributed the regulations to the commanders of the brigades. Did you communicate with the brigade commanders?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI
utterances.text: This document was sent to the brigades accompanied by the order of the commander of the NLA and, at the same time, I communicated them via telephone.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: How often would you communicate with the brigade commanders, General?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI
utterances.text: Compulsory communication occurred two times a day, in the morning and in the evening, when they were obliged to report for the developments. But also there were contacts upon needs and upon the situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Thanks, General.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Could we please call 65 ter 778.6, and I hope it will be tab 5, Your Honours. If we could go to the first page of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Tab 5. May I inquire, Your Honours, if tab 5 is the same as on the screen. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Are you looking maybe at the Macedonian translation or at the Albanian? It should be the last page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. It is in tab 5.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. They were looking at the Macedonian version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: General, you are asked to move a little bit backwards. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The General needs to try and see the screen, which is difficult for him, and as he is trying to turn the bundle of papers in the binder he is hitting the microphone all the time, so I'll try and have the microphones moved back a little to give you more fighting room, General.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Thanks, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: General, do you see the cover page of this regulation?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: We see -- we can see like in the upper part of the document General Staff, military secret, highly confidential document and the title is: Order on internal life of the NLA. General, did you produce this document, this regulation?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: When did you produce it?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI
utterances.text: Simultaneously I worked on several documents. All of them more or less were prepared in March and April. Some of them were prepared in May as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Of 2001; correct?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI
utterances.text: Yes, of 2001. This document was prepared the last.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: And, General, in order to produce this particular document, in which material or knowledge did you rely on?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI
utterances.text: I worked on such documents earlier as well, but this document helped me the most when I prepared the order on the internal life of the Kosovo Protection Corps, because the soldiers lived in barracks. I used the existing regulations of the Yugoslav army and the army of Albania.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Once it was produced, General, to which units within the NLA did you distribute this regulation?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI
utterances.text: To all the brigades.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Could we please go to page 2 of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: And, General, which was the main purpose of this regulation?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI
utterances.text: This regulation was aimed at settling certain issues which should be settled by means of regulation. We have here shelter, how barracks are built, the building itself, the yard, the dormitory, and so on. So the aim of this regulation was to regulate these issues, because at the time when we were preparing to hand over our weapons, during the Essential Harvest operation, we asked for certain barracks to be given to us, in order to put there some of our soldiers but this did not happen. So this served, more or less, to the conditions at which the NLA operated at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Thanks, General. Just to look briefly at page 1. We can read in the first paragraph and I quote: "On the basis of past experience and to recognise the NLA, thereby applying more concrete measures and activities in a uniform manner, I hereby order as follows." And, indeed, we see in item 1, lodgings and regulations. And number 1, barracks; number 2, the grounds of the barracks; number 3, buildings and facilities. Could we please go briefly to page number 7. It's page number 6 of the hard copy.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: General, do you see as item 2 internal regulations for the unit?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Let me find it first. I found it.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: We can read in number one, daily regulations in the unit. The first paragraph reads, and I quote: "In order to unify all activities and to establish order and discipline in all the structures of the NLA, the commanders are to set up a schedule for all activities within a 24-hour period in accordance with plans approved in advance by the General Staff." General, is this an example of an issue that needed to be regulated?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: I will rephrase it, General. Which is the significance of this particular paragraph?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI
utterances.text: I wasn't following the paragraph. Could you please tell me once again which paragraph it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Yes. It's the first paragraph, just below daily regulations in the unit. Do you wish me to read it again?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI
utterances.text: Yes, please, only that part, the part you just read.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: "In order to unify all activities and to establish order and discipline in all the structures of the NLA, the commanders are to set up a schedule for all activities within a 24-hour period in accordance with the plans approved in advance by the General Staff. Another schedule is to be set up for non-workdays and holidays."

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI
utterances.text: The question?

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Which is the relevance, General, of this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI
utterances.text: This paragraph should be seen in the conditions in which the NLA operated because, as you might know, they were almost all the time in positions and in the context of such conditions it was necessary for the command to draft a plan whereby to divide the activities to be carried out within 24 hours. It is important because, by means of such a plan, the work of the brigade of the units was organised.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will seek to tender 65 ter 778.6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, simply a matter of clarification if we could be assisted by the witness on this point. I think he has indicated early in his evidence that he wasn't sure about the exact date but then he referred to the Operation Essential Harvest and indicated that or, as we understood it, that this may be related to the relevant parts of the regulations concerning barracks and I was wondering whether counsel for the Prosecution could clarify with Mr. Ostreni whether the regulations were drafted during the Essential Harvest operation or at any time before.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that the witness said that he started producing the document between March, April and it was one of the last. The reference to Operation Harvest was on a completely different issue and I think that my learned colleague can actually question this witness in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The witness's evidence was that he produced all of these documents in March and April and some into May and this particular one was the last produced. Nothing as late as Essential Harvest, Mr. Mettraux. There was a references to Essential Harvest but in a specific context. So we will -- it's up to you whether you want to pursue a question of date again or whether you want to move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: I would like to move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: I think that it is clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P499, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Could we please go to tab number 1, which is Exhibit P459. Again, the Albanian version will be the last one. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: General, did you find the first page of this document?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: We can read in the first page, General, NLA, in the upper part of the document, personnel and material formation of the brigade, and then we see on the lower part, on the right side, your name and also 2001. General, did you produce this regulation?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: When did you produce it?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI
utterances.text: It's not a rules, it's a formation; I want to make a correction. I drafted it at the General Staff where I worked.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: When, General? When did you draft it, when did you produce it?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI
utterances.text: As I already stated, I worked constantly with such documents. Therefore, it is very hard for me to clearly state which one was done when. But, in general, I may say that I worked on them during the period of March, April, and in May I submitted them.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Thanks. General, in order to produce this document, did you rely in any particular prior regulation? Which source did you use?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI
utterances.text: In order to prepare the formation, I already resorted to my very long experience. I had the opportunity to work at -- [indiscernible] at the communal staff level. Then I worked all the formations of the Kosovo Protection Corps so base on all this experience and on documents that I used to possess during -- in the course of my experience, I worked to compile such a document.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: General, to whom did you -- once you compiled this document, to whom did you distribute this document?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI
utterances.text: The document was sent to all the brigade commanders operating in -- at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: In order to expedite the proceedings, General, all the documents that you produced, all the regulations or formations that you produced, to whom were they distributed?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI
utterances.text: To the commanders of the brigades of the NLA.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: If we could go, please, to the second page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: General, we see here a chart with the title personnel and material formation of the brigade. The chart contains different columns, positions according to the formation. First name and last name, date of birth, rank, general, high ranking officer, officer, uniforms and then weapons. Which was the purpose of this document, General?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI
utterances.text: The purpose of this document was to regulate the organisation -- organisational chart of the brigades so that there were -- there was room for name, last name, date of birth, in that chart, for them not to need any duplicates.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Could we please move to tab number 2, which is Exhibit P416.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do you want to tender tab 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: It is already an exhibit, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. What is the number; do you know?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: And now I am moving to tab 2, which is already an exhibit, Your Honour, P460.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: General, you have in front of you an another document, again NLA General Staff, in the upper part of the document approved by NLA commander Ali Ahmeti. The title reads: Personnel and material formation of the infantry battalion and the date is 2001. General, did you produce this document?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: When did you produce it?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI
utterances.text: I prepared this document before I did that on the brigade command. I worked on this personnel and material formation of the infantry battalion. It was done during the period I mentioned earlier, from March to end of April.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: In order to produce this particular document, did you rely on any particular source?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI
utterances.text: On my experience during which I constantly had under my command battalions. Therefore it was not difficult for me to produce such a document, because I already had an idea of what a squad looked like or what three squads looked like which formed a company, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: If we could go, please, to page 6 of this document, and in the hard copy it will be the ERN R062-6673. It's almost at the end of the Albanian version.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: General, we have a chart in front of us which reads: Personnel and material formation of the infantry battalion. Which was the purpose of this particular chart?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI
utterances.text: The table that we discussed earlier is a collective one. This is an individual table. Therefore, it indicates all the units that form this battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: If we could go, please, to page 2. It would also be page 2 in the Albanian version.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: General, this chart reads: Mobilisation plan of the infantry battalion. We have different columns as well. Unit, number and name of the unit, venue or location, responsibility, total in uniforms, weapons. Which is the purpose of this chart, General?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI
utterances.text: This shows the development of mobilisation of the infantry battalion, during which we have put notes on the collective composition of the battalion so that the command -- commander knows what the composition of his battalion is.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: General, I don't quite understand one of your -- one point of your answer, "during which we have put notes on the collective composition of the battalion." Could you please clarify what do you mean with that?

utterances.speaker: GZIM OSTRENI
utterances.text: This chart shows that here above there is the command of a battalion, for example, which is composed of one officer, another deputy, and six soldiers. And eight uniforms, one pistol, one automatic rifle. So these are data that show not to whom they belong, for example to the commander or to someone else, but it's a collective data. And then you see offices and so on, for example, sabotage surveillance unit, for example, the 1st Corp, 13, so it is a collective data. The second is 10. The 3rd Squad, I think, has 10. So the total number is 43 soldiers and one officer. These are collated data for the brigade commander to know what's going on in his brigade. Just number -- they are simply figures, not personal data. If the commander wants to know, he has all the available data to know what's going on. When it come to the personal data, then you had data for each and every one of the soldiers and officers.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Thanks, General.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: That would be a convenient time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, we -- are you wanting to tender tab 2 or are you continuing?

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: It's already an exhibit, Your Honour. It's P460. Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That brings us to the end of our time today. As I've mentioned earlier, we are not able to sit tomorrow to allow another trial to be sitting. We haven't enough courtrooms. So that we resume on Thursday morning at 9.00 to continue the evidence. Thank you. We adjourn now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 8th day of November, 2007, at 9.00 a.m. 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.01 p.m.,
